title: Did Date Masamune Really Wear a Burial Robe to Meet Hideyoshi?
description:
The story as it is usually told: at Odawara in Tenshō 18 (1590), the late-arriving Date Masamune came before Toyotomi Hideyoshi dressed all in white (shishōzoku, burial clothes), his hair tied with mizuhiki cord, and Hideyoshi touched his neck with a cane and said, "Any later, and it would have been dangerous." This episode opens the records one at a time, in the order we opened them.

Masamune's own letters: on the 6th day of the 6th month (the day after he arrived) he writes "so far, things look all right," and also "I don't know how it will go"; on the 12th, "everything was done just as I wished"; on the 14th, that he was received on the morning of the 9th, invited to tea on the morning of the 10th to see famous pieces, and that Hideyoshi talked with him warmly about rare swords and wakizashi. Date Shigezane's Date Nikki and the Sendai domain's Teizan-kō Jike Kiroku (1703): he was lodged at Sokokura in Hakone; on the 7th, five men including Seyakuin Zensō and Asano Nagayoshi came to question him, and his men feared he would be ordered to commit seppuku; at the audience Hideyoshi pointed his cane at the ground and at Odawara Castle; the Jike Kiroku says only that he tied his hair with mizuhiki and "looked strange." The line about the neck comes from a memoir by the Kaga samurai Sekiya Masaharu, as retold by Maeda Shichirōbei, who heard it from the next room. In the Edo-period Ujisato-ki, the shishōzoku belongs to a different summons the next year (1591), and the book itself marks it "so it was said"; the Meishō Genkōroku gives Masamune's own account of a gold brocade armor surcoat. The earliest work we found that puts mourning clothes at Odawara is the 1934 Ugoku Nihonshi; the 1937 Nihontō Monogatari says shishōzoku. In 2022 the Mainichi Shimbun reported Hagiwara Daisuke's finding that no reliable source supports the burial clothes.

Conclusion: none of the 1590 letters or Date clan records opened here mentions white clothes, so that file is closed; who first put the burial robe at Odawara is still open (postwar novels, a 1942 film and undigitized books were not checked). Dates follow the old lunar calendar: the 9th day of the 6th month is July 10, 1590 (Gregorian). The age of 24 is counted the traditional East Asian way. Sentences beginning "we think" are this channel's view.

The illustrations in this episode were generated with AI. The historical figures are cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant as likenesses; modern researchers and actors are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-20

dm101.text: Summer 1590, outside Odawara Castle. Hideyoshi's camp is still laying stone walls.

dm102.text: The story goes like this: Date Masamune, very late, has finally arrived.

dm103.text: Age 24, all in white: shishōzoku in Japanese, a burial robe;

dm104.text: his hair tied with the thin paper cord used to wrap gifts, called mizuhiki.

dm105.text: Hideyoshi, on his stool, taps Masamune's neck with a cane:

dm108.text: That month, Masamune wrote letters himself. What did they say?

dm109.text: A century later, the Date clan's history also recorded how he was dressed.

dm110.text: Who wrote down the words about his neck?

dm111.text: And the burial robe: who was the first to write it in?

dm112.text: Did Masamune really meet him in a burial robe?

dm201.text: One of those letters is dated Tenshō 18, sixth month, sixth day.

dm202.text: He writes: I arrived yesterday, the 5th, and people came out to meet me;

dm203.text: So far, things look all right.

dm204.text: Then the tone shifts: some matters the regent hasn't raised, nor has he.

dm205.text: Who knows how it will go.

dm206.text: Our affairs are known up top, and talked of down here;

dm207.text: if something goes wrong, there's no predicting it.

dm208.text: But Hideyoshi has sent for Asano Nagayoshi and Maeda Toshiie to be his "guides";

dm211.text: On the 12th, to a retainer: the regent showed him every favor;

dm212.text: everything was done just as I wished.

dm213.text: Within a day or two, a guide would lead him home, straight through Kantō.

dm215.text: Two days on: he met Hideyoshi the morning of the 9th;

dm216.text: on the 10th, he was invited to tea and shown famous pieces.

dm217.text: Hideyoshi warmly talked him through rare swords and wakizashi.

dm218.text: The same letter says Ōshū's 54 districts and Dewa's 12 were left to him;

dm219.text: Aizu became the regent's land only "for now."

dm220.text: We think each letter sounds more relaxed than the last.

dm221.text: From worry to pride: where was he in the days between?

dm301.text: At Sokokura, a hot-spring village in Hakone.

dm302.text: Hideyoshi had him lodged up there on arrival.

dm304.text: he left only in month five, via Echigo and Shinano.

dm305.text: His chief retainer, Date Shigezane, later wrote:

dm306.text: Shut away in these hills, his men all worried.

dm307.text: On the 7th, five envoys came: Seyakuin Zensō, Asano Nagayoshi and others.

dm308.text: The records don't even name two of them.

dm309.text: Asano was the "guide" from the letter.

dm312.text: and the Ashina had already paid respects, yet he'd seized their Aizu.

dm315.text: The Date records agree: an order to commit seppuku.

dm316.text: A clan history compiled later adds one more thing:

dm317.text: He told the envoys: I hear Rikyū came; I'd like a tea talk.

dm318.text: What did Hideyoshi make of that?

dm319.text: A country lord with such taste: a man like that won't rebel.

dm320.text: Hearing his defense, Hideyoshi said: it seems everyone hates Masamune; but that Aizu affair was still too rude.

dm321.text: The verdict: Aizu, Iwase and Asaka taken away; his old lands kept.

dm322.text: Remember the "for now" in his letter? Aizu went to Gamō Ujisato.

dm323.text: The Date records put it before the meeting.

dm324.text: So how was he dressed that day?

dm401.text: The Date clan history was only compiled in 1703; the mizuhiki from the start is in it:

dm402.text: It says he looked very strange.

dm403.text: Ieyasu, Toshiie and other lords sat beside Hideyoshi.

dm404.text: As he withdrew, Hideyoshi pointed his cane at the ground: come.

dm405.text: Halfway, Masamune remembered the wakizashi at his waist.

dm407.text: He tossed it to Hideyoshi's scribe, Waku Sōze, and went up.

dm408.text: He pointed at the castle: its walls, and how to take it;

dm409.text: Masamune answered freely, with his own views.

dm411.text: Shigezane's memoir says all praised him: a country man, yet unafraid.

dm413.text: he heard the scene later from Waku Sōze.

dm414.text: Waku Sōze, the teller, later became a Date retainer.

dm415.text: Yet neither book says the cane touched his neck.

dm416.text: So where does the tap on the neck come from?

dm417.text: That opening line is in the memoir of Sekiya Masaharu, a Kaga samurai.

dm418.text: Here the order differs too: pleased, Hideyoshi saw him at once.

dm419.text: Hideyoshi: false beard, a three-foot red-sheathed sword, a thin cane;

dm420.text: Masamune hid a small wakizashi in his robe, to stab Hideyoshi if he could.

dm421.text: But Hideyoshi poked his neck with the cane;

dm422.text: All thought of murder gone, his neck felt scalded.

dm423.text: Then Hideyoshi took him hawking and had him carry his sword; he thought: now I'll be favored.

dm424.text: And where did Sekiya hear this?

dm425.text: The book says Masamune told it himself to Kaga's lord, Maeda Toshitsune;

dm426.text: but the one who heard it was Maeda Shichirōbei, in the next room.

dm428.text: Did Kaga hand down only this Masamune version?

dm429.text: No. Kaga had another story too: the same line,

dm430.text: with a samurai named Tsuda Tōtōmi poked in the neck.

dm431.text: By 1935, a teachers' guide to school history said: Hideyoshi tapped his neck with the cane,

dm433.text: And the shishōzoku from the start: where is it in Edo books?

dm501.text: The next year, another case: Tenshō 19, summoned to Kyoto for trial.

dm502.text: The Edo-period Ujisato-ki says that time he wore shishōzoku,

dm503.text: and had a gold-leafed pillar carried before his horse.

dm504.text: At the end it adds: "so I heard."

dm505.text: What did later books put him in at Odawara?

dm506.text: The late-Edo Meishō Genkōroku has Masamune's own account:

dm507.text: Leaving most of his men, he wore a gold brocade armor coat to Hideyoshi.

dm508.text: Spotting him, Hideyoshi called: Lord Date, is it? Come here.

dm510.text: white raw silk painted with gold and red clouds, and leopard-skin hakama.

dm511.text: So when did the burial robe finally go on?

dm512.text: The earliest we found: a 1934 popular history by the Social Education Society:

dm513.text: Reportedly, resolved to die, he came in mourning clothes.

dm514.text: A 1937 book on Japanese swords is blunter: shishōzoku.

dm515.text: The 1987 taiga drama Dokuganryū Masamune: its synopsis has the opening scene, white robes and mizuhiki.

dm516.text: A look back at the drama writes: Hideyoshi's cane went "whack" on his neck.

dm517.text: Did anyone ever go back and check?

dm518.text: In 2022, the Mainichi Shimbun reported that this tale, played often in taiga dramas,

dm519.text: per Toyama Municipal Folk Museum curator Hagiwara Daisuke, has no solid source.

dm520.text: Remember the Kaga samurai Sekiya Masaharu? Hagiwara's book is about his Itsuya no Kakimono.

dm521.text: The white robe isn't in his letters or the Date history: file closed. Who first put it on him is still open.

dm522.text: Where did you first see it: a drama, manga, or game?

dm523.text: We only tell what the records hold. Subscribe to open the files with us.
